PROVISION FOR MINIMUM AGES FOR MALES AND FEMALES
speechtext: for leave to introduce Bill No. C-128, respecting marriage (age of marriage).

subtopic: PROVISION FOR MINIMUM AGES FOR MALES AND FEMALES
speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR MINIMUM AGES FOR MALES AND FEMALES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canada has heretofore failed to impose minimum age requirements with respect to marriage as it might have done pursuant to the powers contained in paragraph 26 of section 91 of the British North America Act 1867. At present in various Canadian provinces children may contract marriage at ages substantially below what has been considered an appropriate minimum age by numerous delegates to the United Nations, namely 15 years.
This bill is designed to strengthen and dignify the institution of marriage by fixing an absolute minimum age of 16 years for males and 15 years for females below which no person in Canada may enter into this solemn contract.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

subtopic: HAL BANKS CASE-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Before the orders of the day are called I wish to ask leave to move the adjournment of this house in accordance with standing order 26, in order to discuss a matter of urgent public importance, namely the threat to law and order which is inherent in a statement as reported in the press made by Mr. James Todd, secretary treasurer of the Canadian maritime union. He has charged, according to press reports, that certain people in the government made a deal with Hal Banks to get him out of Canada. He is further reported to have said that Banks was only charged with offences for which he could not be brought back; they did not want Banks back to tell everything he knows.
Furthermore, as appears from the report, the F.B.I. in the United States was not requested by the Canadian government for assistance in locating the said Hal Banks, and generally that incomplete and evasive answers and explanations given to this house by members of the government reveal a failure to deal forthrightly with the case of Hal Banks, which failure has resulted in Banks being free to flout the law and escape justice thereby bringing into disrepute the administration of law and justice.

I should like to say, in response to my right hon. friend's intention to move the adjournment of the house, that under our rules it is obligatory to establish a number of preliminaries. My right hon. friend, while he has brought forward a matter that is, of course, of public importance, has not established the urgency that is contemplated within our standing orders. In any event, even if there were the kind of urgency that is contemplated within the standing orders, the matter can be dealt with more effectively later, in view of the fact that the government will bring in the estimates of the Department of Justice not later than Thursday of this week.
In addition, the responsible minister, the Minister of Justice, is now engaged in conference on constitutional questions with the provincial attorneys general, who have assembled here and began meetings this morning. They will continue to meet throughout today and tomorrow. The Prime Minister likewise, as my right hon. friend will recall, left a short time ago for Charlottetown to meet Her Majesty the Queen.
But I suggest, in addition to the fact that the Minister of Justice is not here, being preoccupied with important business having to do with constitutional matters involving relatiens with the provinces, arid also because this question, important as it is, does not come within the rule of urgency, that my right hon. friend has not made a case for disturbing the order of business for today. Further, I give him the assurance that he will have the opportunity of dealing with this matter not later than Thursday of this week, when the estimates of the Department of Justice will be before the house.

Mr. Speaker, I thought I was steering clear of the merits, just as my hon. friend so often does in his own arguments on questions of this nature. I had not at all mentioned the merits of the statements made. I was simply reiterating the words contained

I further suggested to Your Honour that the proper course to follow would be to accept that urgency attaches to this matter; because after all, if Mr. Todd's statements which have been read into the record by the Leader of the Opposition are true then the matter is indeed one of urgency, because it holds up to contempt the administration of law and justice in this country. I would think that all members of the government would want to see discounted any reflection on the government that there has been connivance with the S.I.U. in Mr. Banks' escape from Canada, and the only way in which this can be done is by allowing the house to debate this subject at the earliest possible opportunity.

subtopic: PROVISION OF CREDIT FOR PURCHASES BY SYNDICATES

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Tuesday, September 29, consideration in committee of Bill

No. C-121, to provide for the extension of [DOT]credit to farm machinery syndicates-Mr. Mays-Mr. Lamoureux in the chair.
On clause 2-Definitions.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: PROVISION OF CREDIT FOR PURCHASES BY SYNDICATES
speechtext: Shall clause 2 carry?

subtopic: PROVISION OF CREDIT FOR PURCHASES BY SYNDICATES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, when the committee was considering this bill last week hon. members raised a number of questions, and if the committee is agreeable I think it would save time and satisfy most of their objections if I were to make a short statement at this stage dealing with the matters already raised.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: PROVISION OF CREDIT FOR PURCHASES BY SYNDICATES
speechtext: Is this agreeable to the committee?

subtopic: PROVISION OF CREDIT FOR PURCHASES BY SYNDICATES
speechtext: Agreed.

subtopic: PROVISION OF CREDIT FOR PURCHASES BY SYNDICATES
speechtext:
We are dealing with clause 2, but since it is closely related to clauses 3 and 9 I hope hon. members will permit me to refer to whatever extent is necessary for clarity, to those clauses as well.
Several hon. members have questioned the provision in the bill that the definition of farm machinery should be set by regulation instead of being spelled out in the bill. There are excellent reasons and excellent precedents for this approach. The main reason, as I should think lawyers would understand better than anyone else, is to ensure the greatest possible flexibility in the use of this legislation.
I think most informed persons recognize that to define is to limit. I admit right away that a definition set by regulation could turn out to be just as limiting as a definition set by parliament, but if a definition set by regulation does turn out in day to day experience to be faulty, then it can be revised and broadened a lot faster than if it were set out by law. If, for example, we did write a legal definition of "farm machinery" into this bill, what if it overlooked three or four machines which turned up in loan applications a week after the bill became law? The only way these machines could then be made eligible would be to come back to parliament and go through the whole process of having this bill amended. Even then there would be no way of being sure that we would not run into a similar situation the week after such an amendment had been passed.
I think all hon. members should be able to see from this how much more flexible the administration of this legislation will be by leaving the definition to be set by regulation.
Farm Machinery
By leaving the definition up to the administration of this legislation we are making it possible for the definition to be revised according to day by day experience, and to be revised quickly and easily.
That is the main reason for taking the approach we have. But there is also a very good precedent for taking this approach, a precedent already approved by parliament and well proven in actual operation. This is the precedent we find in the Farm Credit Act. In section 19 of the Farm Credit Act the definition of "farm equipment" is left to the regulations. I am sure all hon. members would agree that this approach has proven very successful in the Farm Credit Act, which is a good act. It was passed by the previous government, but it is still a good act and I don't mind saying so.
Mr. Chairman, I ask the committee to let us proceed in the same way with this bill. Because of the need for flexibility in this program, and because of the rapid development of new machinery, a legal definition written into this act now could seriously restrict the adaptability of the program.
Hon. members have also questioned the provision in the bill that the terms and conditions of a syndicate agreement should be set by regulation, instead of being written into the measure as law. Again we believe there are excellent reasons and excellent precedents for this approach. The most obvious reason is that this provides greater flexibility in dealing with farmers' applications for loans under this bill. But a precedent can also be found in the Farm Credit Act, again a precedent approved by parliament and well proven in actual operation. We believe this is the only sound approach we can take to ensure that the program, a new and experimental one, can be revised and improved as experience dictates.
Besides leaving the definition of "farm machinery" to the regulations the Farm Credit Act, in section 11, confers other rather extensive discretion on the Farm Credit Corporation. This discretion, which is not subject to approval by governor in council, includes the authority to prescribe the forms of mortgages and agreements which farmers make with the corporation.
I believe this was one occasion when the previous government showed a lot of common sense. I am convinced, and I am sure everyone familiar with the great variety of the farmers' credit needs would agree, that this kind of flexible approach is essential for success in any farm credit program.

Farm Machinery
This is why we have proposed that the matters to be covered in agreements under the farm machinery syndicates bill should also be left to the administrators, to the people dealing directly with the farmers.
Naturally we have given very careful consideration to the general terms which the regulations will require in the agreements. Farmers forming a syndicate will have to make provision for such items as the rights and liabilities of syndicate members, including the interest in it of each member; insurance of the property against fire, and of the syndicate against public liability; the addition of new members; the withdrawal, death, insolvency, retirement or incapacity of a member for any cause; the dissolution of a syndicate; the holding of syndicate business meetings; the election of syndicate officers; the procedures in the event of default by an individual syndicate member; maintenance and sale of machinery; keeping proper records and accounts.
These are some of the general terms. But I am sure hon. members would not want to dictate to farmers in advance every detail as to how each syndicate must organize to meet these general terms. In administering the program the Farm Credit Corporation will of course suggest various ways in which these general terms can be met. For example, suppose a member wants to withdraw from a syndicate because he has sold his farm, or does not need the machinery any longer for some other reason. The syndicate agreement could include a provision for any member to withdraw as long as he could make a mutually satisfactory arrangement with other members to take over his share of both the assets and the liabilities, or for another farmer acceptable to the other members to take his place. In other words, since he would have an equity in the net worth of the syndicate he would be able to dispose of it to the remaining members or to another farmer.
But farmers themselves might like to make other arrangements. By leaving the terms and conditions of agreements under this bill to be set by regulation, by the administrators, we provide the farmers the freedom to make any reasonable arrangements they and the corporation see fit.
I think it should be obvious that if we tried to fix, by legislation, the exact nature of agreements which the farmers should work out among themselves we would be severely restricting the program and could very sharply reduce its value to our farmers.

Several hon. members have questioned the provision for joint and several liability of syndicate members. This is referred to in clause 3 of the bill. But the question of liability is also inherent in clause 2, because the syndicate agreement as referred to in this clause is in fact a form of partnership agreement with obvious liability implications.
Obviously it is essential that there be some formal agreement among farmers intending to own and operate machinery on a co-operative basis. Several approaches are possible. We could have asked the farmers to form a limited company or corporation. We could have asked that the farmers incorporate themselves as a co-operative. But either of these approaches would have involved a great deal of extra time and expense for the farmers. Either of these approaches would have been clumsy and slow. We want to cut out all the red tape we can in this program. We want to be able to handle the farmers' loan applications just as quickly as possible.
Both these approaches are obviously loaded with red tape and delay, especially for small farmers who might only want to get together to buy one or two machines. We do not mind seeing lawyers make a decent living. I have known lawyers who are very nice people. Some of my best friends are lawyers. But this is legislation for the farmers, and we have done our best to make it as simple and convenient as possible for the farmer to use.
The Farm Credit Corporation will, of course, be in a position to suggest the form of a general agreement which farmers may follow in setting up a syndicate. If a large number of farmers decide to set up a syndicate to share a large amount of machinery where a lot of money is involved they may want to hire a lawyer to help them. But in most cases we believe the farmers, in consultation with the Farm Credit Corporation, should be able to draw up the necessary agreements without legal advice.
We tried to imagine, for example what farmers in the Atlantic provinces would say if we asked them to form a company just to buy a potato planter or a potato digger; or if we asked farmers on the prairies to form a company just to buy a grain cleaner or a grain dryer. It seemed to us that the best, the simplest and most convenient approach was to require only that farmers set themselves up in a partnership agreement to borrow under this legislation.

Partnerships are regulated under provincial law, and in its lending operations under this program the Farm Credit Corporation will operate within the scope of provincial laws. It may help if I point out that farm machinery syndicates in Britain were organized by the farmers and the farmers' unions, and that the farmers themselves, after looking into this very thoroughly themselves, decided from the start that making individual syndicate members jointly and severally liable was one of the most important factors in ensuring the success of these syndicates.
We have a Reading University report on British farm machinery syndicates which says "The key to the problem of credit was the joint and several liability of the participating farmers working together in owning and operating a particular machine as a specific and restricted partnership." These British farmers saw for themselves that if they were going to work together in this way they would also have to share the financial responsibilities. I think our farmers are just as bright as British farmers and just as capable of understanding this. In fact I am sure no Canadian farmer would want to go into one of these deals unless he was sure his partners were going to have just as much at stake in the success or failure of the deal as he had.
And, after all, how much risk is this going to involve? I think hon. members should remember that ordinarily the assets of one of these syndicates will always be greater than its liabilities. These loans will cover only 80 per cent of the machinery cost from the start, so the assets of a syndicate will be greater than its liabilities from the beginning. With regular repayments slightly higher than the rate of depreciation for the machinery the assets should be worth more than the balance of the loan right through until the loan has been paid off. Furthermore, the fact that a syndicate's members know they are jointly and severally responsible is obviously going to do a lot to ensure that every member sees that the machinery is well maintained. They will all own it, and every one of them will understand very well, I am sure, that keeping it in good shape is the best way to protect their individual interest in the syndicate.
I know farmers pretty well. I don't think any of them are going to enter one of these deals without sizing up their partners pretty thoroughly. I think the judgment each farmer exercises with respect to his prospective partners will probably be the best guarantee we
Farm Machinery
can have that these syndicates will be a success.
In other words, Mr. Chairman, after the most careful consideration the government feels certain that the joint and several liability provision will not present any problem to any individual farmer wanting to take part in one of these loans. In fact we think this provision might easily prove to be one of the essential factors in the success of this program by offering some real encouragement to syndicate members to work together and solve in a friendly, neighbourly way whatever problems might come up.
Trying to limit the liability of an individual member to only his individual share in the syndicate poses some serious problems of administration. It would involve far more red tape both for the corporation and for the farmers. It could also open the way to bad situations among members of a syndicate. If something happened to make one member decide he wanted to get out, for example, he could be in a position to tie up all the assets of the whole syndicate if there were only limited individual liability. The corporation, to protect the interests of the taxpapers in recovering these loans, might have to seize the machinery because of bad faith by only one member.
In other words, limiting the liability as suggested by some hon. members could put one individual syndicate member in a position where he could keep all the other members from continuing to use the machinery. By making all syndicate members equally liable no individual member will be in a position to spoil it for the others, if by any chance this kind of a situation did arise. The remaining members could assume the share in both the liability and the assets of a defaulting member, and in this way protect their investment with the least possible trouble.
There could be another real benefit from taking the approach to syndicate liability proposed in the bill. It could very well help some farmers benefit from this type of credit who would not be able to qualify for credit on their own. Consider, for example, the case of a young farmer who has used up all his personal credit in order to get started in farming. His neighbours, who may be well established farmers, know him personally and have a high regard for his ability and integrity. They may be perfectly willing to join with him on a promissory note for one of these loans because they know him. And, because of the faith shown in him by his

Farm Machinery
better-off neighbours, through their willingness to back his credit, the corporation could grant him credit for which, on his own, he would not qualify.
In concluding my remarks on this point, Mr. Chairman, I would like to refer to a suggestion by the hon. member for Acadia that we should not be asking for a promissory note under this bill because it is not required under the Farm Improvement Loans Act. The hon. member is as well informed on this as he is on other matters. Section 9 of the farm improvement loans regulations states very clearly that a promissory note shall be made for a farm improvement loan. In fact, as anyone who has ever borrowed from a bank should know, it is common banking practice to require a promissory note from any borrower. I think I should also point out that when two farmers join to obtain a farm improvement loan to buy machinery, they are held jointly and severally responsible for repayment of the loan.
Mr. Chairman, I feel sure we can satisfy any further objections raised by hon. members as the committee continues its examination of this bill. I appeal to all hon. members that they then let this bill pass and give the farmers a chance to try this out. Let us give our farmers a chance to test this new program in action. The farmers of this country are the only ones who can put this bill to the real test.

subtopic: PROVISION OF CREDIT FOR PURCHASES BY SYNDICATES
speechtext:
We have all listened with great interest to what the minister has just said. I am afraid if the answers and explanations he will be asked to give later on are no better than those he has just given, the bill is likely to encounter considerable difficulty.
I wish to take up the first point the hon. gentleman made. I speak not only as a lawyer-I plead guilty to that charge-but as one who farmed actively for eight or nine years before I became a member of this house. That was at a time when it was necessary to be a lawyer or an auctioneer to have enough money to be able to carry on farming operations.
The reasons given by the minister for not spelling out in detail, as far as possible, the meaning of what is contained in this legislation are the same as have been advanced year after year by officials of provincial and federal governments. They say, in effect "We know best. Leave it to us. If changes are required we will make the changes." I do not deny there are certain occasions in this complex and fast moving world when it is

necessary to have power to make regulations as far as the machinery of legislation is concerned. Nevertheless, other considerations should apply to the basic essentials.
The minister has referred to clauses 2, 3 and 9; I hope I will have the same latitude accorded to me. With regard to these provisions I say that more than regulations are necessary. Even if this were the best government in the world-and we on this side, at any rate, have some doubts about that

I did not come here to allow the views of the government to be substituted for my own. I must say I have a good deal more confidence in the Farm Credit Corporation than I have in the government. My experience with that body has been excellent. The way they have operated, the co-operation I have received, and the way in which they have dealt with farmers has been such that I have a considerable amount of confidence in them. But I was not elected as a member of parliament to give this government a blank cheque for $25 million when the very basic essentials which comprise the heart of this legislation have not been clearly shown to us. This is where I make my stand.
I recognize that it will always be the function of the executive to initiate legislation, to bring it forward. This is not the function of a legislative body. It is for us to examine and analyse the legislation to see that it is complete, that all the essentials are there to make the legislation effective, worthwhile, and do that job it is supposed to do. I have strong doubts as to whether this is the situation here.

That is what I am doing, Mr. Chairman, and that is what I have been doing. We have been listening to insinuations and smart aleck quips from a bunch of trained seals who know nothing and care nothing about this bill. They have made little or no honest contribution to our consideration, with the exception of one hon. member who offered his opinion in complaint about the interest rate. He suggested that the interest rate should be stated, and that the bill ought to make clear what interest is payable. I value his opinions very much. I do not think the rates should be more than the 5 per cent charged by the Farm Credit Corporation. He is the only member from that side of the house who has made any contribution. The rest have just made smart aleck quips, which is indicative of their lack of interest in the plight of farmers across Canada.
Mr. Chairman, I asked the minister two questions. The last one was this: If I joined a syndicate and the total value of my assets was $15,000 would the corporation consider my promissory note in the amount of $45,000 of any value. The minister indicated that the corporation would not consider it of any value. He said that whether or not I received a loan would depend upon the situation and circumstances of the other members of the syndicate. In other words, what he has said is that unless I have unencumbered assets to the value of the requested loan my application would not be considered favourably. By the admission made a few minutes ago, the minister has confirmed my earlier fears, that it will only be wealthy farmers who will be able to take advantage of the provisions of this legislation.
If a syndicate desires to borrow $45,000, that syndicate must be formed of individual farmers who have assets to the total value of the loan required, and those assets must be unattached in any way. I suggest there are not very many farmers who own unattached assets of that value. I suggest that limitation in this bill is its ruination, and that is why I said very little in respect of the bill until this afternoon when we reached consideration of clause 3. Clause 3 says that each man must sign a promissory note for the total amount owing by the syndicate. In other words, in order for me to join a syndicate with seven other members and borrow $100,000 I must have assets and security 
worth $100,000. Otherwise any other bank or lending institution can attach my goods.
Someone said earlier that one can borrow $55,000 from the Farm Credit Corporation under part III loans, $15,000 from the bank under the Farm Improvement Loans Act, and can then join a syndicate and as a partner in that syndicate borrow the maximum of $15,000. This makes a total debt of $85,000. But if the man joined a syndicate with seven other members and the syndicate borrowed the maximum amount he would then have to have a total net worth of $100,000. If we add to that the $55,000 that can be borrowed from the Farm Credit Corporation and the $15,000 under the Farm Improvement Loans Act, this means that the man will have to have a net worth of $170,000 in order to join a syndicate of that size.
Members on the other side say that this legislation is for the small farmers, the family farm. They will have to bear with me. I come from a part of Alberta where there are many small farmers. Their net worth is not too large and I should like to see them be able to take advantage of this legislation which the house has approved in principle, if it is at all possible for them to do so. I have studied the bill and have talked to various farmers in my constituency about it. I have deliberately talked to those farmers who I felt needed to enlarge their present holdings. I have talked to those farmers who I felt should have more money made available to them as a working tool to enable them to enjoy a standard of living comparable with that enjoyed by workers in other industries in Canada.
When I came to clause 3 and told them that as it now stands they would have to sign a promissory note making themselves liable for the total amount owed by the syndicate, they immediately threw up their hands and said that their banker knew how large a promissory note they could sign. He was familiar with their net worth statements. In other words, they doubted very much whether the corporation would be much more lenient than the banker in this regard.
I may have criticized the bill but I do not wish it to be taken that I am criticizing the management of the Farm Credit Corporation.
I think they have done a tremendous job. My constituents feel that the corporation has done a tremendous job. I have no complaints at all about the administration of that act. Let me make that abundantly clear.
But here we are dealing with the question of security. It has been my experience and

that of my constituents that the Farm Credit Corporation, to put it mildly, must have all kinds of security before they will make money available to an individual farmer to enlarge his holdings or buy a new farm. So I am somewhat dubious that this clause really adds anything to the bill. The minister has said that it must be there. He did not really explain fully why it must be there. He said that such a clause is always required in the case of most corporations and limited companies, but not necessarily all of them. He said that a farmer has to sign a promissory note when he obtains a farm improvement loan. He went on to explain that if a promissory note was not signed by each individual member of the syndicate for the total amount borrowed, then in the event of the death of one member the machine would be claimed by the Farm Credit Corporation and this would tie up the whole operation of the machine until it was cleared by the remaining members of the syndicate. In my view that was a rather weak defence of this clause.
I believe that if a promissory note is necessary at all each man should only have to sign for his proportionate share of the loan obtained by the syndicate. In other words, if three farmers join together and borrow $45,000 each should only be asked to sign a promissory note for $15,000. If seven farmers join together and form a syndicate and borrow $100,000 each, one would then sign a promissory note for a little under $15,000. Surely I do not have to go into detail with regard to the difference between approximately $14,000 and $100,000.
Members of the legal profession in this party and in the New Democratic party have pointed out the legal complications in which this clause as worded would involve many farmers. It is all well and good for the minister to say that the farmers know one another and they would not join a syndicate where there was some doubt with regard to one member's character. This may be all well and good. The farmers know one another and are good judges of character, I believe, but this will not stop complications arising in the event of a death. In addition, one member could get into many financial difficulties in his own activities outside of the syndicate, thus placing himself in a dangerous position in regard toi the syndicate.
The minister has accused me of being partisan in this debate. He has accused me of playing petty politics. If I have appeared to do so it is because of the plight of the small farmer. If I have appeared to seem annoyed

at the irresponsibility of some of the Liberal backbenchers it is purely because at times I have felt I am fighting in a lost cause, in trying to make this bill applicable to small farmers generally and, perhaps a bit selfishly, to the farmers of my riding particularly who have faced untold difficulties in years gone by. One could consider the area in Alberta in which they live to be a drought area which has been severely stricken by harsh weather conditions. While I may have appeared to be partisan at times in this particular debate, I would not want to be interpreted in that way. I was partisan on behalf of the small farmer, and the small farmer only. I am sure that my constituency is not the only one in Canada that has farmers in it facing unusual elements such as hail, drought, long distances from markets and so on. I am sure there are other constituencies in which farmers are in similar positions. I am sure there are other constituencies, the farmers in which can take advantage of the principle of this legislation, and join together.
I mentioned in some of my earlier remarks that I had joined in three different groups of my neighbours and bought farm implements, small implements. Farmers are not denied the opportunity of coming together and buying larger implements such as those envisaged by the minister in this bill. I sincerely want this bill made applicable to those small farmers of whom I speak. I do not care how they vote, what their politics are. My sole aim in being in this house is to try to better their condition. With this thought in mind I find that clause 3, subclause (2), paragraph (a) is in direct conflict with the aims and aspirations of many small farmers.
In an earlier speech I mentioned that a small farmer with assets of $20,000 will not sign a promissory note for a syndicate requiring a loan of something like $80,000. He will not mortgage his farm, his livelihood and his children's future by signing a promissory note for a syndicate composed of similar small farmers. No farmer is afraid of his own worth. No farmer is afraid to sign a note for a proportionate share of a syndicate loan. With this in mind I should like to move an amendment to this clause. I know there may be objections to the amendment from the other side of the house. I ask members on the other side to forget partisan politics and to weigh the virtue of this amendment. I ask them to think of the farmer with assets of $15,000, to whom I referred a short time ago. I ask them to recall that the credit corporation will not

Put yourself in the position of a farmer with assets totalling $15,000. You feel that you could use more money, and perhaps you could, with the advice of a farm leader. I use that term rather loosely, but there is always a leader in any farm community. Perhaps if you could join a syndicate with him he could show you how to use this capital in a way that would permit you to secure a better standard of living.
While in some former speeches I have found this bill slightly objectionable, I think perhaps it could be of benefit to the small farmers in my constituency and in many parts of Canada. Without further ado I am going to move:

"be liable for his proportionate share of the outstanding amount of the loan."
This is the amendment I wanted to move. I do not want any hurried answer from the minister. Previously in this debate I have wished the minister would quickly rise to his feet and put me straight if I was in error. I do not want any hurried answer. I should like this subject talked about by some of the learned counsel on the other side. I should like the minister to consider the amendment and to think of the small farmers who do not have extra credit facilities available to them. I want him to think of the small farmer whose total assets may be only $15,000. Surely we as legislators should make this bill applicable to him. This is all I am saying: Surely, we should try to make this bill applicable to him. Has the farmer a bad record in putting up security to the Farm Credit Corporation? He has not; he has a very good record. Under the Farm Improvement Loans Act his record could not be better; and so I ask, why do we have to be so cautious? Why can't we bend a little toward aiding the small farmer?
I plead with the minister to give this serious consideration, because as the bill is worded I am convinced, particularly in the light of the answers he gave to my questions when I started to speak, that this bill by its provisions will exclude many small farmers who are in need of help. I suggest the minister give this more thought and that his learned parliamentary secretary, who has a great deal of farming experience and who has dealt with a lot of small farmers throughout his lifetime, should also give it a great deal of thought. I do not exclude the chairman of the Farm Credit Corporation from this suggestion, because time and time again the corporation has been confronted with the plight of the small farmer. Do not forsake the small farmer in passing this legislation.

This clause provides that every loan shall be secured by, first a "promissory note", and second by "such other security" as the corporation may require. With regard to the first security, the promissory note, the provision is that this promissory note will require each member to undertake severally and jointly responsibility for the amount of the loan. I have listened carefully to the minister both this afternoon and this evening but I have not yet heard a satisfactory explanation of why the farmers who join a syndicate must accept joint responsibility. The minister has quoted from the British experience, and the farmers there seem to prefer it. He has also said something about the fact that no one farmer should be able to tie up the other farmers in the syndicate.
I must confess that I am not impressed with his argument. I am convinced that by requiring these farmers to accept joint responsibility as well as several responsibility you will make it extremely difficult for a lot of farmers to join these syndicates. If there are four farmers who are going to go together to form a syndicate and would be entitled to borrow up to $60,000 provided they purchased $75,000 worth of machinery, you see the liability that a member of that syndicate is assuming. First of all, he must put up his share toward providing $15,000 worth of cash for the 20 per cent equity in the machinery which the members must have in the first place. Then he must sign a note not only for his $15,000 but for the entire $60,000 which the syndicate are borrowing from the Farm Credit Corporation. If a farmer assumes this liability, how is this going to affect the credit of any member? What are his chances of ever borrowing from anybody else under any other circumstance? When a possible lender looks over his financial position and sees that he has signed a note for $60,000 for which he may be liable, this is not going to make him a very likely person

to whom anyone else would extend further credit. I do not know why the minister insists on joint liability. It seems to me that the Farm Credit Corporation is adequately secured if each farmer assumes responsibility for his share.
In the case of the instance I cited before, all four farmers who borrowed $60,000 would each be then responsible for $15,000. Remember that the Farm Credit Corporation has $75,000 worth of machinery as security plus "such other security" as referred to in paragraph (b), to which I will come in a moment. It seems to me that they are adequately safeguarded if the members of the syndicate assume several responsibility without being required to assume joint responsibility. I think that this will keep a lot of farmers out; they will be afraid that signing a note, which could be for as much as $100,000, would be so onerous that it would completely destroy their credit and their capacity to borrow anything in the future from any other agency.
The second thing about which I have some misgivings, and I would ask the minister if he can to clear this up for me, is this. The second security which the Farm Credit Corporation will take under paragraph (b) is-

My remarks tie in with the nature of the security that is being requested in clause 3, as well as with the amendment put forward by the hon. member. I wonder if the minister appreciates the situation with regard to the type of security he is going to be enforcing as it applies across Canada. We know that the promissory note is a joint and several one. I do not agree with the minister as to what several liability means. In other words, if I am potentially liable on a note for $75,000, that is the fact in which the man I go to see is interested. Am I possibly going to be liable for $75,000? The minister must agree that is a possibility.
However, I am not sure that the minister, even though he comes from Alberta, is fully aware of the complications that arise under the chattel mortgages act of that province in connection with enforcing a security. This is not going to be a conditional sales agreement proposition because the Farm Credit Corporation will have to take a chattel mortgage on the machinery. Under the chattel mortgages act of the province of Alberta, if you are going to proceed under a chattel mortgage, the chattel mortgage is limited to the machinery in question. You must elect

to proceed under either the chattel mortgage or the promissory note. If you proceed under the chattel mortgage to seize the machinery, then any unrealized balance on the forced sale of that machinery goes by the board.
Let us, for example, say that a machine worth $60,000 was purchased by paying 20 per cent down. There will be $40,000 on the chattel mortgage. Suppose the chattel mortgage is reduced to $35,000 and difficulties arise so that the corporation must realize on its chattel mortgage. Then, the machinery is only worth $25,000. I will tell the minister that under the law of Alberta the corporation will be stuck for $10,000 because it cannot then proceed personally against the makers of the note. On the other hand, if the corporation decides it is not going to move under the chattel mortgage but proceeds on the note, it obtains a judgment. Then the corporation could not attach any of the machinery in question because the provisions of the chattel mortgages act are immediately brought into play. This act limits the corporation, as a judgment creditor, to the value of these particular goods. Of course they are subject to the exemptions act of that province.
I am describing a condition that applies particularly to the province of Alberta. I am mentioning this because the corporation, in order to get the proper amount of security, will insist on something more than a chattel mortgage.
